overview: This file consists of a three-page consular despatch reporting an October 1937 attempt by the Dairen postal authorities to prevent an American firm from sending letters to China. After Fraser Federal representative William A. Morgan’s mail to Tientsin was rejected because it was written by a foreigner and was not in Japanese, American Consul Stuart E. Grummon raised the matter with the Kwantung territorial administration and Communications Bureau chief Toshiyuki Ito, citing possible infringement of the 1911 U.S.–Japan Treaty of Commerce and Navigation. Ito denied that such interference was authorized and ordered the matter corrected, although evidence collected by the consulate suggested that the prohibitory notice had originated with the Communications Bureau itself.

subfiles.title: Despatch on attempted interference with an American firm’s mail to China
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports and protests the Dairen postal authorities’ refusal to accept correspondence sent by an American business representative to his firm’s office in Tientsin.
subfiles.summary: On October 20, 1937, Dairen postal employees refused registered and unregistered letters that William A. Morgan of Fraser Federal wished to send to Tientsin, asserting that correspondence from a foreigner to a foreign firm in China had to be written in Japanese. Grummon raised the issue with the territorial government as a possible violation of the 1911 U.S.–Japan Treaty of Commerce and Navigation, but officials claimed that they lacked authority over the Communications Bureau. Bureau chief Toshiyuki Ito denied that mail from Americans to China was prohibited and ordered officials to correct the situation after Grummon described a posted notice restricting mail to China to Japanese senders. The consulate nevertheless received information suggesting that the notice had originally been posted on instructions from the Communications Bureau.
keywords: Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of 1911

interest: The despatch provides a compact case study of wartime interference with foreign communications in Japanese-controlled Manchuria and of American efforts to defend treaty and commercial rights. Particularly revealing is the discrepancy between Ito’s formal denial of any restriction and the consulate’s evidence that the Communications Bureau had ordered the prohibitory notice. The document also illuminates the fragmented authority of the Kwantung administration and preserves the distribution network through which American diplomatic posts across Japan, China, and Manchuria shared such reports.
